In its constructive forms, it has united peoples for liberation and self-determination, from India’s nonviolent resistance to colonial rule to the Baltic states’ peaceful exit from the Soviet Union. Even the American Revolution was born of a desire for sovereign civic identity. But nationalism becomes a threat when it favors purity over cooperation and elevates isolation over shared interest.

History underscores this point. In the early twentieth century, surging nationalism coincided with weak economic ties between rival powers. When a Serbian nationalist assassinated Archduke Franz Ferdinand in 1914, it lit the fuse of a continent already soaked in competitive militarism, ethnic strife and imperial ambition. There were no significant trade relationships to act as a restraint.

efforts to bind nations together economically, particularly in Europe.
The European Coal and Steel Community, which evolved into the European Union, was designed
precisely to make war not just undesirable but unprofitable.
France and Germany, historical adversaries, became economic partners.
Even Brexit, though politically dramatic, did not sever the United Kingdom’s deep trade links with the EU. Economic detachment is far harder than political slogans suggest.

The global financial crisis of 2008 offers another critical data point. It exposed deep vulnerabilities in the world economy, triggered mass unemployment and brought entire financial systems to the brink. Yet even then, great powers did not resort to war. Instead, they pursued coordinated bailouts, G20 summits and transnational fiscal rescue.
The logic was clear: economic entanglement

Yet this logic often breaks down in countries less tied into global systems. In Ukraine, over sixty-seven thousand people died in 2024 alone. More than 150,000 have been killed in Sudan. Gaza has lost tens of thousands. Millions have been displaced. These conflicts are not just humanitarian crises. They are signs of a weakening global fabric.
The countries most prone to war are often those most economically disconnected. Without strong interdependencies, the incentives for restraint collapse.

Some argue that globalization empowers authoritarian regimes by making them richer, more connected and harder to isolate. But isolation rarely moderates behavior. If anything, it removes consequences, making aggression cheaper and less visible.

At the same time, globalization itself is changing. Automation and AI are reducing dependence on cheap labor and global supply chains. Trends like reshoring and friendshoring are bringing production back within political alliances. If economies rely less on international labor or manufacturing, they may have fewer reasons to maintain peace through cooperation. Economic fragmentation is not just an ideological concern. It is a strategic one.

The financial landscape is shifting as well. China’s digital yuan has already processed nearly one trillion dollars in cross-border transactions. BRICS nations are developing alternative payment systems and debating a shared reserve currency. Africa’s Pan-African Payments and Settlement System has reduced dollar dependence for regional trade. As financial systems diverge, coordinated responses to global crises become harder to execute. Sanctions lose power. Diplomacy loses leverage. If the U.S. dollar loses its status as the backbone of global trust, the world may face more than monetary instability. It may lose one of its last tools of unified restraint.

None of this is to suggest that nations should tolerate authoritarianism or abandon human rights in the name of commerce. Engagement is not endorsement. The goal is not to trade with dangerous regimes without scrutiny but to understand how entanglement, economic, technological, and informational, can restrain them.

Containment becomes possible without immediate escalation.

Still, globalization is not only about trade. Cultural interdependence is growing too. Social media, global entertainment and shared digital spaces are creating a cultural commons that transcends borders. A song released in Seoul can trend in São Paulo. A viral video from Nairobi can spark discussion in New York. This connectivity builds empathy, awareness and shared experience. It makes it harder to turn a blind eye to suffering and in some cases, harder to start a war without scrutiny. But even this cultural web remains uneven. Over two and a half billion people still lack internet access. Expanding connectivity is not only an economic goal. It is a peace strategy.
Globalization has not been without cost. It has amplified inequality and fueled populism. In some cases, it has strengthened authoritarian regimes. But
dismantling global ties would only replace flawed dependence with dangerous unpredictability.
The challenge is not whether to integrate, but how to do so wisely.
